summary:
Scan In Space is a web app for exploring NASA SPHEREx observations over time. It lets users look at the same part of the infrared sky across different dates, compare images, and investigate moving or variable objects.

You can search by object name or coordinates, or select a location directly on the sky map. The app retrieves the relevant SPHEREx observations, aligns them, and provides tools for blinking between images, stacking exposures, and subtracting observations from different dates.

It also includes photometry, spectral analysis across SPHEREx's 102 wavelength bands, proper-motion measurements, light curves, and cross-matching with astronomical catalogues. By combining SPHEREx with older 2MASS and WISE observations, we can examine changes over roughly 26 years.

We designed the interface for both casual exploration and more detailed analysis, with downloadable results and an MCP server for AI-assisted searches.

We tested the pipeline on all five challenge targets and compared its measurements with published astronomical data.
details:
Overview

Scan In Space is a web platform for viewing and analysing time-series observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission.

SPHEREx surveys the sky in 102 near-infrared wavelength bands, covering 0.75–5 µm, and revisits the same regions roughly every six months. We wanted to make it easier to compare these observations over time without manually downloading and processing the original data.

The app allows users to select any position on the sky, browse the available observations, and examine changes between different visits. Alongside image comparison, it provides tools for measuring brightness, analysing spectra, and identifying moving or variable objects.

Data processing

We created a local index of approximately 1.6 million SPHEREx Level 2 files from the DR1/QR3 releases. This allows us to find relevant observations quickly, with typical lookup times around 90 ms in our tests.

Images are accessed directly from NASA's public S3 bucket. Using HTTP range requests, we retrieve only the data needed for a selected region instead of downloading complete files. We also support IRSA services as an alternative data source.

The processing pipeline:

  1. Retrieves the available exposures for a selected position.
  2. Aligns the images to a common coordinate grid.
  3. Groups observations by visit and combines exposures from each detector.
  4. Applies quality masks and outlier rejection.
  5. Produces images that can be compared, stacked, or subtracted.

We also account for proper motion when processing observations of fast-moving stars.

Analysis tools

Besides displaying images, Scan In Space includes several analysis features.

Photometry and spectra

We use the effective point-spread function and per-pixel wavelength information from SPHEREx observations to estimate source brightness and construct spectra. The spectral analysis includes template matching for stars and brown dwarfs, as well as features associated with molecules such as H2O, CH4, CO, and CO2.

Motion and variability

Users can estimate proper motion, generate light curves, and search for periodic brightness variations using Lomb–Scargle periodograms. We also compare detections against Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, 2MASS, and SIMBAD.

Long-term observations

We integrate historical data from 2MASS, AllWISE, and NEOWISE. This extends the available time baseline back to 1999, making it possible to compare positions and brightness over approximately 26 years.

Moving objects

For comets and asteroids, we use IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool to locate relevant observations. The app can align images around a moving object, subtract the background sky, analyse its brightness, and export measurements in ADES format.

Candidate search

The platform includes tools for finding moving objects, variable sources, and unusually red candidates. We use a real/bogus classifier to help separate potentially interesting detections from image artefacts.

Testing and results

We tested the analysis pipeline on all five targets provided in the challenge.

  • Barnard's Star: Recovered its motion with a positional difference below 0.6 arcseconds relative to the Gaia prediction. Its position changed by approximately 4.4 arcminutes between 1999 and 2026.
  • ε Indi B: Identified as a T dwarf, including methane absorption near 3.3 µm. Measured proper motion of 4.4 arcseconds per year, compared with approximately 4.7 from Gaia.
  • WISE 0855−0714: Detected its infrared signal at 3.8–5 µm despite a nearby star approximately 8 arcseconds away.
  • R Draconis: Estimated a variability period of 236–247 days, compared with approximately 245 days reported in the literature.
  • RW Aurigae: Measured an approximately twofold decrease in brightness at 4–5 µm over one year.

In our tests, flux calibration also agreed with 2MASS measurements within 0–3%.

These results are based on known objects rather than new discoveries. They provide a way to check the accuracy of different parts of the pipeline.

Interface

The website has two modes.

Explore mode is intended for users who want to browse the sky without needing much background in astronomy. It includes explanations, a guided tour, and a small discovery game.

Research mode provides detailed measurements, uncertainties, quality flags, and export options in FITS, CSV, VOTable, and ADES formats.

Both modes use an interactive sky map built with Aladin Lite. Users can share links to specific locations and analysis results.

AI integration

We developed an MCP server with 20 tools for searching observations, retrieving images, running analyses, accessing catalogues, and exporting results.

This allows AI assistants to work with the same data and analysis tools available through the website. In one test, an agent searching a field identified ε Indi B as its strongest moving-object candidate.

Technical implementation

The backend uses Python, Astropy, Photutils, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI, and asynchronous I/O. More expensive processing tasks run in separate processes.

The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Aladin Lite.

We use caching to reduce repeated data retrieval and have deployment configurations for Docker and Railway. The project also includes Cloudflare R2 integration and an MCP server.

Limitations and future work

The current version has a few limitations.

Most fields have only three or four SPHEREx visits available so far, which limits some types of time-series analysis. Saturated sources require different photometry methods, and some measurements are only relative.

We also haven't confirmed any new astronomical objects. The candidate search tools can highlight interesting sources, but those still require further verification.

As more SPHEREx observations become available, we plan to use them to improve motion measurements, variability analysis, and candidate searches.

Our main goal is to provide a convenient way to work with SPHEREx data, whether someone wants to browse the infrared sky or carry out a more detailed investigation.
